title: Okpa
localName: Okpa — okpa di oku, okpa wawa
author: Chidinma Eze
desc: Bambara nut flour steamed in leaf wraps for at least an hour — done when it is solid all over, and yielding twelve medium wraps.
longDesc: Okpa is a steamed pudding of bambara nut flour and it is the breakfast of Enugu, so strongly associated with the Ninth Mile Corner that the place and the food are named together. Four hundred and fifty grams of flour, three quarters of a cup of red palm oil and a tablespoon of salt go into lukewarm water, wrapped and steamed for at least an hour. The seasoning is deliberately minimal to let the beans taste of themselves. Note the water figure: the ingredient list says one litre, but the page states 1.2 litres twice and says plainly that 1.2 is the quantity for the perfect texture.
ingredients: 450 g okpa flour (bambara nut flour), 1 lb or 3 1/2 cups
1.2 litres lukewarm water — see the note on the two figures
Banana or uma leaves, or foil
equipment: Banana or uma leaves, or foil
steps: Put the okpa flour in a large bowl and add the palm oil, working it in so the flour takes up the oil evenly.
Add the lukewarm water gradually, mixing all the time, until you have a smooth batter with no lumps.
Add the salt and the habanero pepper to taste, and mix again.
Spoon the batter into leaf wraps or foil parcels and seal them.
Arrange the parcels in a pot with water at the base, not covering them.
Cover and steam at least 1 hour.
The okpa is done when it is solid all over.
chefTips: Work the palm oil into the dry flour before any water goes in. It coats the particles and stops them lumping.
Lukewarm water, added gradually. Hot water starts to cook the flour as it goes in and gives you lumps you cannot remove.
Solid all over is the test — not firm at the edges and soft in the middle. Press the centre of a parcel through its wrapping.
At least an hour. The source says 'at least', and under-steamed okpa is wet and grainy.
Keep the seasoning minimal. Bambara nut has a distinct flavour and the dish is built to show it off.
Water at the base of the pot, never over the parcels.
Twelve medium wraps is the stated yield from 450 g, which makes this a batch worth making for a week of breakfasts.
commonMistakes: Using hot water, which lumps the batter.
Adding the water before the oil.
Steaming for less than an hour.
Letting the water cover the parcels.
sources: Adapted from 'Nigerian Okpa, Okpa di Oku, Okpa Wawa', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 450g okpa flour (1lb or 3 1/2 cups); 3/4 cup red palm oil; 1 tablespoon salt; habanero pepper to taste. YIELD AS PRINTED: 12 medium wraps. COOKING TIME AS PRINTED: 'At least 1 hour.' DONENESS CUE AS PRINTED: 'The Okpa is done when it is solid all over.'

A THREE-WAY CONTRADICTION ON THE WATER, within the single page, reported and not reconciled. The ingredient list says '1 litre (4 cups) hot water'. The preparation notes say 'Prepare 1.2 litres of lukewarm water'. The cooking directions say '1.2 litres of water is the quantity of water you need for the perfect Okpa texture'. So the page states 1.2 litres twice and asserts it is the correct figure for texture, while the ingredient list's 1 litre is the lone outlier — and the two also disagree on temperature, hot against lukewarm. The 1.2 litres lukewarm is used above because the page's own emphasis points that way, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than hidden.
Headnote, as printed: an Eastern Nigerian delicacy made from bambara beans, famously associated with 9th Mile Corner near Enugu, with minimal seasoning to preserve the beans' natural flavour.

A SECOND, INTERNALLY CONSISTENT SOURCE for comparison: 'How To Make Okpa (The Original Recipe)', byline 'Published by Claret', thecuriouskitchen.blog — 4 cups okpa flour to 4 1/2 cups lukewarm water, a ratio consistent between its list and its method; 1 cup palm oil; 1/2 teaspoon ground uziza seeds; salt; pepper; banana leaves. Steaming 45 minutes to 1 hour on medium heat. Cues: 'firm to touch', 'separates easily from the leaf', 'a toothpick inserted comes out clean.' Yield 5-6 wraps.

CAUTION ON THAT SECOND SOURCE, and why its quantities are not used above: 'Claret' is a single first name on a recent personal blog with no verifiable bio. It is not blocklisted and the recipe is internally coherent, but it does not meet the named-author bar applied throughout this collection. It is cited here only for corroboration, and the corroboration is useful: its 4 cups to 4 1/2 cups works out close to 1 : 1.1 flour-to-water, which independently supports All Nigerian Recipes' 1.2 litres over its own 1 litre.

The extra cues from that source — separates easily from the leaf, toothpick comes out clean — are not reproduced in the steps above since they belong to the unverified source, but they are consistent with 'solid all over'.
storage: 4 days refrigerated in the wrapping, 2 months frozen.
reheating: Steam 10 to 15 minutes, or microwave in the leaf.
healthBenefits: Bambara nut is high in plant protein, fibre and lysine.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
Low glycaemic index and naturally gluten-free.
culturalNote: Okpa and the Ninth Mile Corner outside Enugu are so tightly linked that the stretch of road is known for it — travellers stop to buy wraps still hot from the pot. Bambara groundnut is an underused African legume, drought-tolerant and high in protein, and okpa is the dish that makes the best case for it.
